# Second Mandingo War

The Second Mandingo War (1891–1895) was the second of the three Mandingo Wars fought between French colonial forces and the Wassoulou Empire led by Samori Touré. It occurred during the Scramble for Africa and formed a decisive stage in French expansion in inland West Africa.
Background
By the late 19th century, Samori Touré had established the Wassoulou Empire across parts of present-day Guinea, Mali, and Côte d’Ivoire. French expansion into the interior intensified as part of broader colonial competition for control of trade routes and territory in West Africa.
Earlier diplomatic arrangements between France and Samori’s state deteriorated as French military outposts advanced inland, leading to escalating conflict.
Campaign phases
Initial French advance (1891)
The campaign opened on 10 March, 1891 when French forces under Colonel Louis Archinard advanced from Nyamina toward Kankan. This phase included the capture of Kankan and the destruction of Bissandugu, the former Wassoulou capital.
Battles of 1892 and strategic withdrawal
In 1892, French forces fought Wassoulou troops at Soumbe Creek and Diamanko Creek. Despite strong resistance, Wassoulou forces were forced to withdraw under sustained French pressure.
Samori Touré then initiated a strategic eastward retreat and adopted mobile warfare and scorched-earth tactics. French forces under Pierre Humbert consolidated captured territory and established fortified positions.
Continued campaign (1893–1895)
By 1893, Wassoulou forces had lost key territory and supply networks. French columns captured remaining administrative centers such as Faranah and expanded control across Upper Guinea.
By 1894–1895, Wassoulou authority in the western region had largely collapsed, marking the end of sustained resistance in the Mandingo theatre.
Key battles and events
* Capture of Kankan (1891)
* Fall of Bissandugu (1891)
* Battle of Soumbe Creek (1892)
* Battle of Diamanko Creek (1892)
* French consolidation of Kérouané (1892)
* Eastward withdrawal of Wassoulou forces (1892–1893)
* Capture of Faranah (1893)
* Collapse of Wassoulou authority in Upper Guinea (1893–1894)
* French advance toward the Kong region (1894–1895)
Casualties
Precise casualty figures are unknown. French records provide only qualitative descriptions of losses. Fighting at Soumbe Creek and Diamanko Creek resulted in heavy casualties on both sides, but no reliable totals survive.
Modern historians note that colonial reporting often undercounted African losses and inconsistently recorded French casualties.
Aftermath
The war resulted in the fragmentation of the Wassoulou Empire and the loss of its core territories. French control expanded across much of Upper Guinea.
It marked a decisive phase in French West African expansion and preceded the final defeat of Samori Touré in 1898.
